workload: 64KB unique model-output tail (stream-watch size) whose 60-char windows never repeat, so the scan stores every offset.
notes: The non-loop path, which is what every stream tick hits until a real loop appears, does text[i:i+60] for each offset and keeps those str keys in one dict (~61k live objects, ~8MB) until return. A rolling hash keyed by start index, comparing characters only on a hash hit, returns the same boolean without retaining a string per offset. Five separate process runs were identical.

workload: 8000-paragraph .docx (word/document.xml ~1.3MB) of plain section text, the stdlib extractor read_file uses for Word.
notes: ElementTree.fromstring keeps the whole document tree (one w:p/w:r/w:t node set per paragraph) alive while the text is joined, so peak is ~10MB for ~0.9MB of extracted text. iterparse that clears each paragraph after its text is taken returns the same string and drops the tree. Overlap: tools/read_extract.py has no commit since 2026-10-12; no open PR mentions read_extract; dexhunter #64366 and #60339 do not touch it. Five process runs were identical. tests/tools/test_read_extract.py covers the docx byte-for-byte text, including the stdlib path.

workload: One large no-$ref tool schema: 500 object groups x 20 described string fields, prepared the way a Gemini parametersJsonSchema request is.
notes: The function copy.deepcopy's the schema and then _inline_refs walks it into a second tree. _inline_refs already returns new dicts and does not mutate its input, so on the success path (no bad $ref) the deepcopy is a full extra tree held as the walk's root. Building the result from the original and copying only in the ValueError fallback keeps the returned schema and the caller's object unchanged. Peak here is ~4.5MB of that double tree. Five process runs were identical.
